title: The collection and grading of representative grain and oilseed samples

lessons.title: Why representative samples matter
lessons.html:
A small sample decides a big payment

When a farmer delivers a truck of maize, wheat, sunflower or soybeans to a silo, the whole load is graded on a sample of a few kilograms. The grade determines the price, whether the load is accepted and where it is stored. If the sample does not represent the load, either the farmer or the buyer loses money. A crop produce analyst must therefore take samples that truly represent the consignment.

Why grain is not uniform

  • Segregation: when grain flows into a truck or bin, fine material, broken kernels and light foreign matter collect in some places, and whole kernels roll to others.
  • Layering: a truck may be loaded from different fields or bins, so quality varies from top to bottom.
  • Hot spots: moisture or insects may affect only part of a load.

A single scoop from the top of a truck is never representative.

The legal basis

Grain and oilseed grading in South Africa is done according to grading regulations made under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990. The regulations for each crop define classes and grades, the deviations to be determined, the sampling requirements and the methods. Always work from the current regulations for the crop concerned; they are updated from time to time.

Sampling equipment

  • Probes (spears): manual or pneumatic probes that take grain from the full depth of a truck or bag.
  • Automatic samplers on conveyors that cut across the full stream at intervals.
  • Dividers, such as riffle dividers, that reduce a large sample to a smaller one without bias.
  • Containers and labels that keep samples secure and identifiable.

Safety at the intake

Climbing onto trucks, moving vehicles, pneumatic equipment and grain dust all carry risks. Use platforms and fall protection where provided, stay clear of moving vehicles, wear a dust mask and never enter a bin or silo.

lessons.title: Collecting and grading the sample
lessons.html:
Taking the sample

  1. Identify the consignment: truck registration, delivery note, crop, producer.
  2. Probe the load at the number of points and in the pattern prescribed for the crop and vehicle, covering the full depth and different areas of the load.
  3. Combine the probe samples into a bulk sample.
  4. Reduce the bulk sample with a divider to the size required for grading. Never just pour off a portion by hand.
  5. Label and seal the sample; keep a reference portion if your procedure requires it for disputes.

Inspecting before grading

Check for live insects, abnormal smell (musty, sour, chemical), excessive heat, and obvious contamination such as stones, glass or poisonous seeds. Some of these can make a consignment unacceptable regardless of grade, so follow the regulations and your site procedure and inform the supervisor.

Grading determinations

Depending on the crop, grading usually includes:

  • Moisture content, measured with a calibrated moisture meter.
  • Foreign matter and other grain.
  • Defective kernels, such as broken, diseased, insect-damaged, immature or heat-damaged kernels.
  • Screenings passing through a specified sieve.
  • Crop-specific tests, for example hectolitre mass and falling number for wheat, or colour and class for maize.

Use the specified sieves, scales and methods. Weigh fractions accurately and calculate percentages on the correct sample mass. Compare results with the grade limits in the regulations and assign the grade.

Recording

Record each determination, the grade, the date, time and your name on the grading certificate or system. Results must be traceable to the sample and the load.

Accuracy and fairness

Calibrate and check equipment daily, keep sieves clean and undamaged, and do not let pressure from drivers or buyers influence a grade. Your integrity protects both parties.

Key points

  • Grain segregates, so one scoop is never representative.
  • Grading follows regulations under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990.
  • Probe the full depth at prescribed points and reduce with a divider.
  • Check for insects, smell, heat and contamination before grading.
  • Record results traceably and grade with integrity.
